primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Airway inflammation and hyperresponsiveness produce reversible bronchoconstriction, mucosal edema, and mucus secretion, increasing airway resistance especially during expiration.
vignette: A 17-year-old girl has episodic wheezing, cough, and chest tightness triggered by exercise and cold air. Spirometry during symptoms shows airflow obstruction that improves substantially after inhaled albuterol.
lead: Which physiologic abnormality most directly explains the reversible decrease in expiratory airflow?
correct: Constriction of bronchial smooth muscle with increased airway resistance
distractors: Fibrotic thickening of the pulmonary interstitium
Obstruction of a pulmonary artery by thrombus
Failure of surfactant synthesis in type II pneumocytes
distractor_notes: Alveolar septal destruction causes emphysema with largely irreversible airflow limitation.
Interstitial fibrosis causes restrictive physiology and reduced lung compliance rather than reversible bronchospasm.
Pulmonary embolism causes vascular obstruction and V/Q mismatch, not bronchodilator-responsive wheezing.
Surfactant deficiency primarily causes alveolar collapse and reduced compliance, classically in premature infants.
key_expl: Asthma causes episodic reversible airflow obstruction largely through bronchial smooth-muscle constriction and airway inflammation.
objective: Explain reversible airflow limitation in asthma through increased airway resistance from bronchoconstriction.

sources.title: Asthma
sources.support: NHLBI describes asthma as chronic airway inflammation with narrowing and hyperresponsiveness that causes episodic reversible breathing symptoms.

sources.title: Asthma
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes airway swelling and tightening of surrounding muscles as major contributors to asthma symptoms.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Loss of alpha-1 antitrypsin leaves neutrophil elastase insufficiently inhibited, allowing proteolytic destruction of alveolar elastic tissue and early emphysema.
vignette: A 34-year-old nonsmoker develops progressive dyspnea. CT shows panacinar emphysema with lower-lung predominance, and serum alpha-1 antitrypsin is markedly reduced.
lead: Excess activity of which enzyme most directly contributes to the lung injury?
distractor_notes: ACE regulates angiotensin metabolism and is not the protease responsible for alveolar tissue destruction in this disorder.
Carbonic anhydrase catalyzes carbon dioxide hydration and is not restrained by alpha-1 antitrypsin.
Myeloperoxidase participates in neutrophil microbial killing but is not the principal protease opposed by alpha-1 antitrypsin.
Cyclooxygenase-2 generates prostanoids and is not responsible for elastin degradation in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.
key_expl: Alpha-1 antitrypsin inhibits neutrophil elastase; deficiency permits excessive elastase-mediated destruction of alveolar walls.
objective: Link alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency emphysema to unopposed neutrophil elastase activity.

sources.title: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes emphysema in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency as resulting from inadequate protection of lung tissue from neutrophil enzymes.

sources.title: SERPINA1 gene
sources.support: SERPINA1 encodes alpha-1 antitrypsin, a serine protease inhibitor that protects tissues from neutrophil elastase.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Diffuse inflammatory injury to the alveolar-capillary barrier increases permeability, causing protein-rich pulmonary edema, loss of aerated lung, and severe shunt physiology.
vignette: A 55-year-old woman with septic shock develops rapidly worsening hypoxemia and bilateral diffuse pulmonary opacities without evidence of left-sided heart failure.
lead: Which pathophysiologic change most directly causes the pulmonary edema?
correct: Increased permeability of the alveolar-capillary barrier
distractors: Increased pulmonary venous hydrostatic pressure from left ventricular failure
Reduced plasma oncotic pressure as the sole mechanism
Obstruction of the main pulmonary artery
distractor_notes: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema is driven by elevated hydrostatic pressure; ARDS is noncardiogenic and reflects permeability injury.
Low oncotic pressure can contribute to edema but does not explain the abrupt inflammatory diffuse alveolar injury of ARDS.
Pulmonary artery obstruction causes perfusion defects, not diffuse permeability edema.
Bronchoconstriction causes obstructive airflow limitation rather than bilateral protein-rich alveolar edema.
key_expl: ARDS is caused by diffuse inflammatory damage to the alveolar-capillary membrane, leading to increased permeability and noncardiogenic pulmonary edema.
objective: Explain noncardiogenic edema in ARDS through inflammatory disruption of the alveolar-capillary barrier.
clues: severe hypoxemia with bilateral opacities and no heart failure

sources.title: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome
sources.support: NHLBI describes ARDS as acute inflammatory lung injury causing fluid leakage into alveoli and severe hypoxemia.

sources.title: Acute respiratory distress syndrome
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes ARDS as severe lung injury in which fluid leaks into alveoli and impairs oxygen exchange.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Embolic obstruction of pulmonary arterial flow creates regions that are ventilated but underperfused, increasing physiologic dead space and causing acute V/Q mismatch.
vignette: A 42-year-old woman develops sudden pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea 5 days after hip surgery. Heart rate is 118/min and oxygen saturation is 89% on room air. Her left calf is swollen.
distractor_notes: Asthma causes wheezing and reversible airflow obstruction but does not fit the postoperative venous thrombosis clues.
Pneumonia usually causes fever, cough, and focal infiltrates rather than sudden dyspnea after immobilization with unilateral calf swelling.
Pneumothorax causes unilateral loss of breath sounds and pleural air; the DVT risk pattern strongly favors embolism.
Pericarditis causes positional chest pain and diffuse ECG changes but does not explain calf swelling and postoperative thromboembolic risk.
key_expl: Sudden pleuritic dyspnea after major surgery with unilateral calf swelling is highly characteristic of pulmonary embolism from deep venous thrombosis.
objective: Diagnose acute pulmonary embolism from abrupt respiratory symptoms plus major venous thromboembolism risk factors.
clues: sudden pleuritic dyspnea with unilateral calf swelling

sources.title: Pulmonary Embolism
sources.support: NHLBI describes pulmonary embolism as sudden pulmonary arterial blockage, commonly from deep vein thrombosis, with surgery and immobility as major risk factors.

sources.title: Pulmonary embolism
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes sudden dyspnea and chest pain from pulmonary embolism and identifies surgery and DVT as important causes.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Glomerular filtration barrier injury causes heavy proteinuria, leading to hypoalbuminemia, reduced plasma oncotic pressure, edema, and compensatory hepatic lipoprotein production.
vignette: A 6-year-old boy develops periorbital and lower-extremity edema. Urinalysis shows 4+ protein without hematuria. Serum albumin is 2.0 g/dL and cholesterol is elevated.
lead: Which syndrome best explains these findings?
distractor_notes: Nephritic syndrome is characterized by glomerular hematuria, inflammatory urine sediment, and usually less severe proteinuria.
Pyelonephritis causes fever, flank pain, pyuria, and bacteriuria rather than massive isolated proteinuria.
Postrenal obstruction causes hydronephrosis and impaired urine flow, not severe hypoalbuminemia from urinary protein loss.
Renal tubular acidosis causes acid-base abnormalities rather than heavy glomerular proteinuria and edema.
key_expl: Heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, and hyperlipidemia define nephrotic syndrome.
objective: Recognize nephrotic syndrome from massive protein loss and its systemic consequences.

sources.title: Nephrotic Syndrome in Children
sources.support: NIDDK describes nephrotic syndrome as heavy proteinuria causing low blood protein, edema, and hyperlipidemia.

sources.title: Nephrotic syndrome
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes nephrotic syndrome as glomerular protein loss associated with edema, low albumin, and high cholesterol.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Mesangial deposition of IgA-containing immune complexes triggers glomerular inflammation and recurrent hematuria, often temporally linked to mucosal infections.
vignette: A 22-year-old man develops gross hematuria 1 day after the onset of an upper respiratory infection. Blood pressure is mildly elevated. Urinalysis shows dysmorphic erythrocytes and red-cell casts.
distractor_notes: Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis typically follows streptococcal infection by a latent period of roughly 1 to 3 weeks rather than occurring concurrently.
Minimal change disease presents predominantly with nephrotic-range proteinuria and edema, not recurrent glomerular hematuria.
Membranous nephropathy is a nephrotic syndrome characterized by heavy proteinuria rather than synpharyngitic hematuria.
Cystitis causes lower urinary symptoms and nonglomerular hematuria without dysmorphic red cells or red-cell casts.
key_expl: Glomerular hematuria occurring during or immediately after a mucosal respiratory infection is characteristic of IgA nephropathy.
objective: Diagnose IgA nephropathy from synpharyngitic glomerular hematuria and urinary red-cell casts.

sources.title: IgA Nephropathy
sources.support: NIDDK describes IgA nephropathy as IgA deposition in glomeruli causing hematuria, often after respiratory infections.

sources.title: IgA nephropathy
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes IgA nephropathy as immune-complex kidney disease associated with blood in the urine around respiratory infections.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Pathogenic PKD1 or PKD2 variants disrupt polycystin-dependent tubular signaling; somatic second-hit events in individual tubular cells can promote focal cyst formation.
vignette: A 42-year-old man with hypertension and bilateral enlarged cystic kidneys has a pathogenic germline PKD1 variant. Only a subset of renal tubules develops cysts.
lead: Which additional event can promote cyst formation in an individual affected tubular cell?
correct: Somatic inactivation of the remaining functional PKD1 allele
distractors: Expansion of a CAG repeat in HTT
Duplication of the normal PKD1 allele
Loss of mitochondrial DNA in all renal cells
distractor_notes: HTT CAG-repeat expansion causes Huntington disease and is unrelated to ADPKD cyst formation.
Duplication of a normal PKD1 allele would not represent the focal loss-of-function event implicated in cyst development.
Global mitochondrial DNA loss is not the characteristic second-hit mechanism in ADPKD.
RB1 activation suppresses cell proliferation; retinoblastoma involves loss, not activation, of RB1.
key_expl: ADPKD is inherited with one pathogenic allele, and somatic loss or mutation of the remaining functional allele can contribute to focal cyst development.
objective: Apply a somatic second-hit model to focal cyst formation in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.
clues: only a subset of tubules forms cysts

sources.title: Polycystic kidney disease
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes ADPKD as commonly caused by PKD1 or PKD2 variants and notes additional somatic changes can contribute to cyst formation.

sources.title: PKD1 gene
sources.support: PKD1 encodes polycystin-1, a protein involved in renal tubular cell signaling and structure.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Loss of the thick ascending limb Na-K-2Cl cotransporter reduces sodium chloride reabsorption, producing salt wasting, secondary hyperreninemic hyperaldosteronism, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, and increased urinary calcium.
vignette: A child has polyuria, poor growth, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, high renin and aldosterone levels, and hypercalciuria. Genetic testing shows biallelic SLC12A1 variants.
correct: Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb
distractors: Na-Cl cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule
Epithelial sodium channel in the collecting duct
Na-glucose cotransporter in the proximal tubule
distractor_notes: The distal Na-Cl cotransporter is defective in Gitelman syndrome, which usually causes hypocalciuria rather than hypercalciuria.
Loss of collecting-duct ENaC causes pseudohypoaldosteronism with hyperkalemia, not hypokalemic alkalosis.
Proximal Na-glucose cotransporter defects cause renal glucosuria.
Aquaporin-2 defects cause nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and water-balance abnormalities without this salt-wasting alkalosis pattern.
key_expl: SLC12A1 encodes NKCC2, the thick ascending limb sodium-potassium-2 chloride cotransporter; loss causes Bartter syndrome type 1.
objective: Relate Bartter syndrome type 1 to loss of NKCC2-mediated sodium chloride reabsorption in the thick ascending limb.
clues: hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with high renin/aldosterone

sources.title: Bartter syndrome
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes Bartter syndrome as renal salt wasting with hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis due to transport defects in the loop of Henle.

sources.title: SLC12A1 gene
sources.support: SLC12A1 encodes the NKCC2 cotransporter that reabsorbs sodium, potassium, and chloride in the thick ascending limb.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Defective proximal tubular and intestinal transport of cystine and dibasic amino acids increases urinary cystine concentration and promotes recurrent cystine stones.
vignette: A 17-year-old boy has recurrent kidney stones. Urine microscopy shows colorless hexagonal crystals.
lead: Which transport defect most directly causes this disorder?
correct: Impaired reabsorption of cystine, ornithine, lysine, and arginine
distractors: Failure of urate filtration at the glomerulus
distractor_notes: Isolated glucose reabsorption defects cause renal glucosuria, not hexagonal cystine crystals.
Increased distal calcium reabsorption would not cause cystinuria and may reduce urinary calcium.
Urate is freely filtered; cystinuria reflects amino-acid transporter dysfunction, not failed urate filtration.
Collecting-duct water-reabsorption defects cause diabetes insipidus rather than selective dibasic aminoaciduria.
key_expl: Cystinuria results from defective transport of cystine and the dibasic amino acids ornithine, lysine, and arginine in proximal tubule and intestine.
objective: Recognize the COLA amino-acid transport defect underlying cystinuria and hexagonal stones.

sources.title: Cystinuria
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes cystinuria as defective transport of cystine and dibasic amino acids causing recurrent cystine stones.

sources.title: SLC3A1 gene
sources.support: SLC3A1 encodes part of an amino-acid transporter involved in renal reabsorption of cystine and dibasic amino acids.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: AGXT deficiency reduces peroxisomal conversion of glyoxylate to glycine, diverting glyoxylate toward oxalate production and causing recurrent calcium oxalate nephrolithiasis and systemic oxalosis.
vignette: A 12-year-old child has recurrent calcium oxalate stones and progressive nephrocalcinosis despite a normal dietary oxalate intake. Genetic testing shows biallelic AGXT variants.
lead: The deficient enzyme normally converts glyoxylate into which product?
distractor_notes: Oxalate is the pathologic product that increases when glyoxylate is not properly transaminated to glycine.
Citrulline is a urea-cycle intermediate and is not the normal AGXT product.
Homocysteine is involved in methionine metabolism and is unrelated to AGXT.
Uric acid is the end product of purine catabolism and is not generated by alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase.
key_expl: Alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase normally converts glyoxylate to glycine in peroxisomes; deficiency increases oxalate formation.
objective: Explain primary hyperoxaluria type 1 through failed peroxisomal conversion of glyoxylate to glycine.
clues: recurrent calcium oxalate stones in childhood

sources.title: Primary hyperoxaluria
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes primary hyperoxaluria as excessive oxalate production due to inherited glyoxylate-metabolism defects.

sources.title: AGXT gene
sources.support: AGXT encodes peroxisomal alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase, which converts glyoxylate to glycine.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: COL4A5 defects disrupt type IV collagen in glomerular basement membrane, cochlea, and ocular structures, causing progressive hematuric kidney disease with sensorineural hearing loss.
vignette: A 16-year-old boy has persistent microscopic hematuria and sensorineural hearing loss. His maternal uncle developed kidney failure at age 30.
distractor_notes: Type I collagen defects cause osteogenesis imperfecta and related connective-tissue disease.
Fibrillin-1 defects cause Marfan syndrome.
Dystrophin defects cause Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy.
Spectrin defects commonly cause hereditary spherocytosis.
key_expl: Alport syndrome is caused by defects in type IV collagen genes, commonly COL4A5 in X-linked disease.
objective: Connect hematuric nephropathy plus hearing loss with type IV collagen defects in Alport syndrome.
clues: maternal male relative with early kidney failure

sources.title: Alport syndrome
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes Alport syndrome as a type IV collagen disorder causing progressive kidney disease, hearing loss, and ocular abnormalities.

sources.title: COL4A5 gene
sources.support: COL4A5 encodes an alpha chain of type IV collagen used in basement membranes including the glomerulus and inner ear.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Loss of AVPR2 signaling prevents vasopressin-induced cAMP generation in collecting-duct principal cells, reducing aquaporin-2 insertion and impairing urinary concentration.
vignette: A male infant has persistent polyuria, hypernatremia, and dilute urine despite elevated plasma vasopressin. Genetic testing shows a pathogenic AVPR2 variant.
lead: Which cellular response to vasopressin is most directly impaired?
correct: Insertion of aquaporin-2 channels into the apical membrane of collecting-duct principal cells
distractors: Insertion of ENaC channels into proximal tubular cells
Activation of NKCC2 in the proximal tubule
Secretion of renin by macula densa cells
Glucose reabsorption through SGLT1 in the collecting duct
distractor_notes: ENaC is expressed mainly in distal nephron principal cells and is regulated primarily by aldosterone; it is not the core vasopressin defect here.
NKCC2 is located in the thick ascending limb, not proximal tubule, and is not directly responsible for AVPR2-mediated water permeability.
Renin release is regulated by renal perfusion, sympathetic input, and macula densa sodium delivery rather than being the principal AVPR2 response.
SGLT-mediated glucose reabsorption occurs in the proximal tubule, not the collecting duct.
key_expl: V2-receptor signaling raises cAMP and promotes aquaporin-2 insertion into the apical membrane of collecting-duct principal cells; AVPR2 loss blocks this response.
objective: Explain nephrogenic diabetes insipidus through failed V2-receptor signaling and aquaporin-2 membrane insertion.
clues: polyuria with hypernatremia and dilute urine

sources.title: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus as renal resistance to vasopressin causing inability to concentrate urine.

sources.title: AVPR2 gene
sources.support: AVPR2 encodes the vasopressin V2 receptor in kidney collecting ducts and regulates water reabsorption through aquaporin-2 trafficking.
